strengths: Introduces a simple, practically relevant way to adapt pretrained protein models to an individual test protein using only the model's original self-supervised objective, without labels or additional homologous sequences.
Demonstrates unusually broad applicability across fitness, structure, and function prediction, covering multiple model families and parameter scales.
The experiments use established datasets and metrics, separate validation data for most hyperparameter selection, multiple random seeds, and explicit precautions against CAMEO checkpoint leakage.

The structure-prediction results on the selected difficult CAMEO targets are meaningful: TTT improves both ESMFold and ESM3 and outperforms the included masked-prediction and iterative-decoding baselines.
The paper is clearly written, motivates the method well, and provides useful implementation and hyperparameter details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Most headline gains outside structure prediction are very small. The strongest ProteinGym result improves average Spearman from 0.4569 to 0.4583; TPS mAP improves from 0.805 to 0.811; and localization accuracy improves from 0.627 to 0.634. No paired tests or confidence intervals over proteins, assays, or folds establish that these improvements are statistically or practically significant. Standard deviations over masking seeds do not capture dataset-level uncertainty.

The structure evaluation is restricted to 18 of 194 CAMEO test targets selected using low baseline pLDDT and high baseline perplexity. This is a relevant diagnostic subset, but it does not substantiate broad claims about structure prediction. Results on the complete predefined benchmark and sensitivity to the filtering thresholds are needed.

Baseline fairness is incomplete. ESM3+TTT evaluates predictions after many updates and selects the iterate with maximum pLDDT, whereas the CoT baseline uses its default eight-step procedure. Comparisons under matched inference compute and candidate-selection budgets are missing, as are standard test-time adaptation alternatives and basic continued-MLM or parameter-update ablations.

The proposed perplexity explanation is weak. Minimizing an MLM loss on the test sequence is expected to reduce a closely related pseudo-perplexity, but this does not imply improved downstream prediction. The paper provides neither a causal argument nor a systematic analysis showing that perplexity changes predict downstream gains; Figure 4 lacks quantitative correlations and uncertainty.

Failure modes are underexplored: TTT degrades several structures and some fitness phenotype/MSA-depth categories, yet there is no reliable criterion for deciding when adaptation should be applied or stopped on tasks without a confidence proxy such as pLDDT.

Novelty is moderate because test-time training with self-supervised reconstruction objectives is established in other domains; the main contribution is its protein-specific instantiation and empirical breadth rather than a new adaptation algorithm.

Reproducibility remains incomplete at submission time: code and dataset-generation scripts are only promised for future release, exact example lists/splits and total computational costs are not fully reported, and several implementation choices lack ablation. These limitations matter because gains are often small and sensitive to hyperparameters.

The claim of a new state of the art on ProteinGym is technically supported by the reported mean but is overstated given the 0.0014 absolute margin, absence of assay-level significance testing, and small degradations in some categories.

strengths: The paper studies a practically relevant problem: adapting pretrained protein models to individual test proteins without requiring labeled protein-specific data.
The proposed procedure is simple and broadly compatible with masked protein language models, and it is demonstrated across fitness, structure, and function prediction rather than on only one task.
The experiments cover several model families and scales, include separate validation data for most settings, and report multiple random seeds.
The appendices provide useful implementation details, hyperparameter grids, per-target analyses, and a newly curated MaveDB validation collection.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the main contribution is a relatively direct application of established self-supervised test-time training to masked protein language models. The claimed perplexity connection largely follows immediately from optimizing the masked-token objective on the test sequence and does not explain why the resulting representation should remain compatible with a fixed downstream head.

The headline fitness gains are extremely small for the strongest models. SaProt-650M improves average Spearman correlation only from 0.4569 to 0.4583, while its MaveDB validation result is unchanged at the reported precision. Calling this a new state of the art and emphasizing a 40% larger leaderboard improvement overstates the practical evidence.

Uncertainty is assessed only over masking/random seeds, producing tiny error bars, rather than over proteins or assays. There are no paired confidence intervals or statistical tests across biological targets, so the significance of improvements such as 0.0014 Spearman, 0.006 mAP, and 0.007 accuracy is unclear.

The structure results are reported only on 18 preselected difficult targets out of 194 CAMEO test targets. Performance on the complete benchmark, including possible degradation on easier proteins, is omitted. The paper therefore does not substantiate broad improvements in structure prediction or provide a validated policy for deciding when TTT should be applied.

The structure comparisons are weak. TTT repeatedly performs gradient updates and downstream confidence evaluation, but it is compared mainly with masked sampling or ESM3 chain-of-thought decoding rather than stronger adaptation, search, retrieval, or equal-compute baselines. Runtime is reported only for ESM3, where the procedure is already roughly 20 times slower than base inference, and the costs for the 3B-parameter ESMFold procedure and other tasks are missing.
The ESM3 evaluation uses a 2022 CAMEO set for a model released and trained later, without a sequence/structure decontamination analysis. This leaves potential benchmark contamination unresolved.

For terpene prediction, the manuscript does not identify a separate dataset for selecting TTT hyperparameters: the same five cross-validation held-out folds appear to support both model selection and the reported aggregate result. Given the small improvement, this possible evaluation leakage is consequential.

The downstream evaluations are narrow and selectively filtered: TPS evaluation retains only low-confidence examples, structure evaluation retains only low-pLDDT/high-perplexity examples, and no broad unfiltered function benchmark is supplied. Such conditioning limits the scope of the central claim that TTT consistently enhances generalization.

The paper acknowledges degradation on some proteins but leaves failure detection and safe deployment unresolved. This matters because downstream ground truth is unavailable at test time and not every task has a reliable confidence measure analogous to pLDDT.

There is an apparent sign error in the fitness description: for log p(mutant) minus log p(wild type), larger positive values ordinarily favor the mutation, whereas the manuscript states that negative values are favorable and positive values disruptive.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the paper promises that a package and some dataset-generation code will be released, but does not provide an available artifact, complete per-task compute accounting, or all details needed to audit the reported results.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically appealing contribution: label-free, per-protein test-time adaptation through the masked-language-modeling objective already available in many protein models. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/c0b5ad500ff6415284519883e907960b/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: the method is evaluated on fitness, structure, and function prediction using several model families and parameter scales, supporting the claim that it is not tied to one architecture or downstream head.

The study generally separates hyperparameter selection from final testing, constructs an independent MaveDB validation set for fitness prediction, uses a leakage-aware ESMFold checkpoint, and reports multiple random seeds.

The structure results on difficult CAMEO targets are compelling: TTT improves both ESMFold and ESM3 over their base versions and relevant inference-time baselines, with several large per-target improvements.

The paper is well organized, motivates the method intuitively through pseudo-perplexity, documents hyperparameter grids and adaptation details, and examines sensitivity, MSA depth, and per-target behavior.
weaknesses: Many headline gains are quantitatively small. For example, SaProt-650M improves from 0.4569 to 0.4583 average Spearman, while the function improvements are similarly modest. Random-seed deviations do not quantify uncertainty over proteins or assays; protein-level bootstrap confidence intervals or paired statistical tests are needed to establish that these gains and the state-of-the-art claim are robust.

The structure evaluation is restricted to 18 of 194 CAMEO test targets selected using baseline pLDDT and perplexity. This is a useful difficult-target analysis, but performance over the full benchmark and the consequences of the proposed deployment-time selection rule should be reported before making broad structure-prediction claims.

Comparisons against alternative adaptation strategies are incomplete. In particular, the paper lacks matched-compute comparisons with homolog/MSA-based self-supervised adaptation, nearby test-time adaptation objectives, and simpler controls that isolate whether improvement comes specifically from fitting the target sequence rather than generic additional optimization or ensembling.

The perplexity explanation is suggestive rather than a substantive theoretical result: reducing training loss on the same test sequence is expected to reduce its pseudo-perplexity, but this alone does not guarantee improved downstream predictions. More rigorous correlation analyses, counterexamples, and failure-mode studies would strengthen the mechanism claim.

The strongest TerpeneMiner system is replaced by its weaker PLM-only variant, and both function and structure experiments focus on preselected difficult subsets. These choices help demonstrate applicability but weaken claims of improvement to the corresponding full state-of-the-art systems.

Test-time computation is nontrivial, failure cases remain underanalyzed, and reproducibility depends on code that is promised for future release rather than currently available. There is also a sign inconsistency around Equation 3: the stated interpretation of positive and negative log-odds appears reversed relative to the formula and later figure captions.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, practically relevant idea: adapting a protein language model to each test protein using its original masked-language-modeling objective while keeping the downstream head fixed.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering structure, fitness, and function prediction across several model families and parameter scales. Improvements are generally consistent across random seeds and independent test sets.

The structure-prediction results on the selected difficult CAMEO targets are promising: ProteinTTT improves ESMFold, HelixFold-Single, and ESM3 and outperforms matched masked-prediction and chain-of-thought baselines.

The authors provide useful implementation details, hyperparameter grids, runtime measurements, LoRA-based scaling to a 3B-parameter backbone, and a separate MaveDB validation collection for tuning fitness experiments.

The analysis indicates where the method is most useful—low-confidence proteins and proteins with shallow MSAs—and the antibody and viral-protein case studies illustrate potentially valuable applications.
weaknesses: The main evaluation is selectively concentrated on examples for which the base model is already known to struggle. The central CAMEO result contains only 18 targets selected using ESMFold pLDDT and ESM2 perplexity, and the function and antibody experiments similarly filter to low-confidence cases. Performance and failure rates on complete, prospectively defined benchmarks are therefore unclear.

Most fitness and function gains are extremely small: for the stronger fitness models the average Spearman improvement is only about 0.0014–0.0044, while function gains are roughly 0.002–0.009. Statistical uncertainty over proteins or assays, effect sizes, and multiple-comparison-aware tests are largely absent. Standard deviations over masking seeds do not capture dataset-level uncertainty.

The claimed new state of the art on ProteinGym is insufficiently supported. The main table compares each customized model primarily with its own base version rather than comprehensively comparing against leading single-sequence, MSA-based, retrieval-based, or protein-specific adaptation methods under matched protocols. It is also unclear whether the reported paired t-test assumptions are appropriate across heterogeneous DMS assays.

The BFVD claim that ProteinTTT 'improves 19% of structures' is not established by structural ground truth. Predictions are selected using the adapted model's own pLDDT, and most validation treats high-confidence AlphaFold2 predictions as references. Correlation between pLDDT and agreement with AlphaFold2 on an easier high-confidence subset does not demonstrate accuracy for the low-confidence viral targets on which the main claim rests.

The proposed justification is largely correlational and partly tautological: training on a sequence necessarily reduces its training pseudo-perplexity, but this does not establish that its downstream representation improves. Controlled baselines such as fitting only the MLM head, parameter-matched adaptation, alternative self-supervised objectives, or explicit wild-type-prior calibration are needed to identify the mechanism. This is especially important for fitness prediction, where training to reconstruct the wild type directly biases log-odds scores against mutations.

Potential leakage is not adequately controlled in the SAbDab case study: no deposition-date or sequence-identity filtering relative to ESMFold's structure-training data is described. The viral evaluation likewise needs experimental structures or temporally held-out references.

The method incurs substantial per-target optimization and model-reset cost. The runtime analysis is favorable relative to AlphaFold2 but does not fully report GPU-hours for large benchmark and BFVD runs or compare accuracy-compute tradeoffs against simply sampling more predictions and other modern folding systems.

There are technical and presentation inconsistencies: the interpretation of the log-odds sign following Equation 5 appears reversed relative to the displayed formula, LDDT is described on a 0–100 scale but tables report 0–1 values, and the appendix contains broken cross-references and the erroneous label 'ProteinPin.'

strengths: The paper explores a practically relevant idea: adapting a protein language model to each target sequence using its original masked-language-modeling objective.
The method is conceptually simple, compatible with several model architectures, and supported by a reasonably clear implementation description and hyperparameter table.

Experiments span structure, fitness, and function prediction, multiple backbone sizes, and several model families. The CAMEO experiments also include compute-matched masked-prediction and ESM3 decoding baselines.

The authors separate hyperparameter tuning from the main CAMEO and ProteinGym evaluations and report multiple random seeds. The antibody and viral-protein studies illustrate potentially useful applications.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is limited: ProteinTTT is essentially established masked-model test-time training applied to protein language models. The paper does not compare against a sufficiently broad set of test-time adaptation, parameter-efficient adaptation, or simple sequence-memorization controls to establish that its particular formulation is necessary.

The central justification is not sound as stated. A cross-protein correlation between low perplexity and good downstream performance does not imply that reducing perplexity by fitting the test sequence causally improves its representation. Single-sequence masked training can simply memorize the wild-type residues, and the paper provides no representation-level analysis or control that separates useful adaptation from memorization.

This concern is especially acute for fitness prediction: the adaptation objective directly increases probabilities of wild-type residues, while evaluation ranks mutations relative to those same residues. A simple wild-type-logit boosting or position-wise memorization baseline is missing. Gains for the strongest models are extremely small (about 0.0014–0.0044 average Spearman), with some phenotype and MSA-depth subsets degrading. Calling the 0.0019 ProSST gain a new state of the art is insufficiently supported by comparisons to the broader ProteinGym leaderboard.

The fitness-score definition contains an apparent sign error: Equation 5 uses log p(mutant) minus log p(wild type), but the text says negative values are favorable and positive values disruptive. This raises uncertainty about score orientation and evaluation correctness.

The main structure benchmark contains only 18 of 194 CAMEO targets, selected using low ESMFold confidence and high ESM2 perplexity. Results are not reported on the complete benchmark, and the ESMFold-selected subset is reused to assess HelixFold-Single and ESM3. This supports a narrow conditional claim, not the broad claim of consistent structure-prediction improvement.

Uncertainty is inadequately characterized. Standard deviations over masking seeds do not quantify uncertainty across the very small set of 18 proteins, and no paired confidence intervals or hypothesis tests across targets are reported. Several conclusions rely heavily on a few very large improvements.

ProteinTTT selects a checkpoint separately for each structure using the maximum pLDDT over many iterations. Because adaptation changes the language-model representations feeding the confidence predictor, pLDDT may become miscalibrated. The paper does not adequately test calibration or compare against equally thorough checkpoint/search controls beyond one masked-prediction baseline.

The BFVD headline claim is not validated against experimental ground truth. An entry is called improved mainly when the adapted model produces higher pLDDT, making the adapted model's own confidence both the selection criterion and principal outcome. Comparison against high-confidence AlphaFold2 predictions is only pseudo-ground truth, and one highlighted PDB example cannot substantiate improvement across hundreds of thousands of proteins. The phrase 'expanding known structures' therefore overstates the evidence.

Function-prediction gains are small, lack statistical tests over examples, and are reported on restricted or potentially reused evaluation data. The TPS experiment filters to difficult examples and reports performance over cross-validation folds that also appear to support model or hyperparameter development, rather than an untouched external test set.

Failure modes and negative results receive little analysis despite observable degradations for some proteins and subsets. Practical cost is also substantial: ESMFold inference grows from roughly 2 seconds to 46 seconds when confidence-based checkpoint selection is used.

Overall, the breadth of experiments is promising, but selective evaluation, weak causal controls, tiny gains on major benchmarks, and the self-confidence-based BFVD analysis leave the central claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: Introduces a simple, broadly applicable test-time customization method for masked protein language models, requiring only the target sequence and leaving downstream heads unchanged.
Demonstrates consistent gains across structure, fitness, and function prediction, spanning several architectures, model sizes, datasets, and five random seeds.
The structure-prediction results are particularly compelling on difficult CAMEO targets, with improvements over masked prediction and ESM3 chain-of-thought baselines.

The antibody and viral-protein case studies illustrate practical relevance, while the MaveDB validation set, MSA extension, runtime analysis, and released implementation strengthen reproducibility and utility.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate: the method largely transfers established masked-model test-time training to protein models. The claimed justification is not a theory of downstream improvement—lower pseudo-perplexity on the same sequence follows directly from optimizing its masked-token loss, but does not imply that an arbitrary frozen downstream head will improve.

Several headline gains are small. On ProteinGym, the strongest model improves from 0.5068 to 0.5087 Spearman, and the function-prediction gains are similarly modest; uncertainty over proteins or assays and effect-size confidence intervals would be more informative than extremely small seed-level standard deviations.

The structure benchmark contains only 18 test targets selected using poor base-model confidence and perplexity. This supports the intended difficult-target setting but does not establish benefit on the full distribution, and pLDDT-based selection across many customization checkpoints introduces extra inference-time selection that should be controlled more carefully.

The claim that 19% of BFVD structures are improved is based primarily on higher predicted pLDDT, not experimental ground truth. Validation against high-confidence AlphaFold2 predictions is circular as evidence of true structural accuracy, and only one example is compared with a PDB structure.

Important comparisons and ablations are limited, including protein-family or nearest-neighbor adaptation, alternative test-time objectives, update-scope and optimizer choices, and compute-matched adaptation baselines. Antibody experiments also omit specialized antibody-structure methods.

There is a sign inconsistency in the fitness section: Equation 5 defines mutant-minus-wild-type log odds, for which favorable mutations normally receive larger values, whereas the text states that negative values are favorable.
